metadata.description: A single IP address as its own record (RFC 8344 / NMstate form) — `address` + `allocation` origin — bound to the interface it is configured on. A static DHCP reservation is just `allocation: static` on this record (ADR-023).

zone.description: WHAT KIND OF NETWORK THIS IS — DMZ, management, internal, storage — as a governed TAXONOMY term (Knowledge.TaxonomyTerm), not a property bundle and not a floor. A CLASSIFICATION, NOT A REQUIREMENT, and the distinction is why this is a taxonomy where `tier` is reference data: a floor is something a second provider can MEET, a category is something a thing IS. Taxonomy is also the only one of the two that carries `normalization_rules`, which is what this needs — providers report `dmz-2`, `DMZ_RESTRICTED` and `dmz restricted`, and all three have to land on one canonical term before any policy can match on it. FOR PLACEMENT ONLY (maintainer ruling 2026-08-10). Nothing critical hangs off a zone directly: it is not an authorization, not a control, and not a boundary. ANYTHING REQUIRED BECAUSE OF A ZONE IS ENFORCED BY POLICY READING IT — the model carries the classification, policy acts on it, which is the same split that governs everything else here. That also keeps the model on the right side of zero-trust architecture, which derives no trust from network location (NIST SP 800-207); UDLM already ships a `zero_trust.posture` setting that a location-as-trust reading would contradict. ON THE BASE though it does not apply to every network type (maintainer ruling 2026-08-10): enough of the family carries a category that the base is the right home, and an element that some types leave unpopulated is what `optional` is for. Scope IS portability (ADR-038 §3) — a category two providers can both report is portable by definition. Provider-reported, like `tier`.

tier.description: HOW GOOD THIS NETWORK IS — a reference to a governed `network_tier`, exactly parallel to `storage_tier`. Each term DENOTES A FLOOR (bandwidth, latency), so asking for a tier is asking for the floor and any network meeting it qualifies: one provider's "10G" and another's "high-throughput" are interchangeable iff both clear it. That is what keeps the intent portable — the match is against the floor, never the string. NAME-SELECTABLE BUT REQUIREMENTS-AUTHORITATIVE (ADR-036, ruled 2026-07-27): a consumer may select by tier name, explicit requirements win where both are given, and the provider records its native class as a realized output rather than something the consumer had to know. ON THE BASE, NOT A TYPE, because performance is expected to be consumable by ALL network class providers and portable (maintainer ruling 2026-08-10). Scope IS portability (ADR-038 §3), so the category base is where a fact every provider must report belongs. Provider-reported at registration or discovery — the party that knows is the one that says.

address.description: The address with prefix as CIDR (RFC 8344/NMstate), e.g. 192.0.2.10/24. Intent for a static reservation; populated at Realized for a dhcp/auto address.

allocation.description: Origin discriminator (RFC 8344 `origin` = NMstate). `static` = a fixed reservation bound to the interface (== a static DHCP reservation); `dhcp` = leased; `link-layer`/`random` = SLAAC/privacy.

relationships.name: attaches_to
relationships.description: attaches_to — the interface this address is configured on. Previously carried as an estate-invented 'assigned_to' note; named from TOSCA AttachesTo when relation names were adopted from standards (common-elements §9).

relationships.name: allocated_from
relationships.description: The pool this address was carved from (mirrors Storage.Dataset.pool → Storage.Pool). Present when the address is allocated from a Network.IPAddressPool rather than statically authored; a realized fact the provider populates, completing allocation-ownership.

adopts.role: relation vocabulary — attaches_to address-on-interface relation name (common-elements §9)
convergent addressing form (address + prefix-length + enabled/dhcp/autoconf) — NetworkManager declarative desired-state

context.purpose: Makes a single IP address its own record — origin, interface binding, and allocation — so each address fact lives in exactly one place.
context.plain_description: One IP address, bound to the interface it is configured on, with how it came to be — `allocation`: `static` (a fixed reservation — this IS the DHCP reservation; there is no second record), `dhcp` (leased), or self-assigned as `link-layer` or `random` (SLAAC/privacy). The `address` itself is CIDR with prefix length — 192.0.2.10/24, never a bare 192.0.2.10. A static record authors the address up front; a dynamic one gets its address filled in once observed. From this one record, projections are derived — a DHCP scope's reservation list, name-side entries — instead of the same fact being retyped per system.
use_when: You need address assignments tracked per interface with their `allocation` origin (`static`, `dhcp`, `link-layer`, `random`).
You need one authoritative record that DHCP reservation lists and other projections derive from.
not_for: The range addresses come from — Network.IPAddressPool.
The subnet's DHCP service configuration — Network.DHCPScope.
The interface itself — Hardware.NetworkInterface; the address attaches to it.
works_with: Hardware.NetworkInterface — the interface the address is configured on.
Network.IPAddressPool — the pool the address was carved from.
Compute.VM — consumers that request or bring addresses.
